extracted.intended_audience: Users of the SINGULAR computer-algebra system (mathematicians and programmers doing computational commutative algebra), especially those using the algebra.lib and assprimeszerodim.lib libraries.
extracted.subtask_description: Reference documentation for SINGULAR library procedures (usage, return values, notes, examples) for tasks such as subring tests, algebraic dependence, kernel computation, (non)injectivity/surjectivity/bijectivity checks, Noether normalization, finiteness tests, and associated-prime computations of zero-dimensional ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: inSubring
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: inSubring(p,i); p poly, i ideal. Return: a list l of size 2, l[1] integer, l[2] string. l[1]=1 iff p is in the subring generated by i=i[1],...,i[k], and then l[2] = y(0)-h(y(1),...,y(k)) if p = h(i[1],...,i[k]). l[1]=0 iff p is not in the subring generated by i, and then l[2] = h(y(0),y(1),...,y(k)) where p satisfies the nonlinear relation h(p,i[1],...,i[k])=0. The proc algebra containment tests the same using a different algorithm, which is often faster. If l[1] == 0 then l[2] may contain more than one relation h(...), separated by comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given with ring and ideal showing output [1]=1 and [2]=y(0)-y(1)*y(2)*y(3)-y(2)^2-1. The displayed behavior is controlled by printlevel >= 0 (default). The returned l[2] is a string representing the polynomial relation; if membership holds, it is expressed as y(0)-h(...).

rubrics_metrics.name: algDependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: algDependent(f[,c]); f ideal (say, f = f1,...,fm), c integer. Return: a list l of size 2, l[1] integer, l[2] ring: - l[1] = 1 if f1,...,fm are algebraic dependent, 0 if not. - l[2] is a ring with variables x(1),...,x(n),y(1),...,y(m) if the basering has n variables. It contains the ideal 'ker', depending only on the y(i) and generating the algebraic relations between the f[i], i.e. substituting y(i) by f[i] yields 0 (the kernel of the ring map K[y(1),...,y(m)] -> basering, y(i) -> f[i]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three different algorithms are used depending on c = 1,2,3. If c is not given or c=0, a heuristically best method is chosen. The basering may be a quotient ring. To access the ring l[2] and see ker you must give the ring a name, e.g. def S=l[2]; setring S; ker;. Example demonstrates setting printlevel, calling algDependent on an ideal and then inspecting ker. Displayed comment appears if printlevel >= 0 (default).

rubrics_metrics.name: alg_kernel
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: alg_kernel(phi,pr[,s,c]); phi map to basering, pr preimage ring, s string (name of kernel in pr), c integer. Return: a string, the kernel of phi as string. If a string s is given, the algorithm creates, in the preimage ring pr the kernel of phi with name s. Three different algorithms are used depending on c = 1,2,3; if c is not given or c=0, a heuristically best method is chosen (algorithm 1 uses the preimage command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that the kernel of phi lives in pr and cannot be returned to the basering; if s is given, the user has access to it in pr via s. The basering may be a quotient ring. Examples show usage mapping between rings and storing the kernel as 'ker' in preimage ring for later inspection. Use setring to inspect the created kernel.

rubrics_metrics.name: is_injective
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: is injective(phi,pr[,c,s]); phi map, pr preimage ring, c int, s string. Return: 1 (type int) if phi is injective, 0 if not (if s is not given). If s is given, return a list l of size 2, l[1] int, l[2] ring: l[1] is 1 if phi is injective, 0 if not; l[2] is a ring with variables x(1),...,x(n),y(1),...,y(m) if the basering has n variables and the map m components; it contains the ideal 'ker', depending only on the y(i), the kernel of the given map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three different algorithms used depending on c = 1,2,3; default heuristically chosen for c omitted or 0. The basering may be a quotient ring; if the preimage ring is a quotient P/I, consider phi as a map from P and the algorithm returns 1 if the kernel of phi is 0 mod I. To access l[2] and see ker you must name the ring: def S=l[2]; setring S; ker;. Example shows returning 0 and inspecting ker which lists relations like y(2)^3-y(1)^2+y(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: is_surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: is surjective(phi); phi map to basering, or ideal defining it. Return: an integer, 1 if phi is surjective, 0 if not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm returns 1 iff all the variables of the basering are contained in the polynomial subalgebra generated by the polynomials defining phi; hence it tests surjectivity in the case of a global ordering. If the basering has local or mixed ordering or if the preimage ring is a quotient ring (in which case the map may not be well defined) then a return value 1 needs to be interpreted with care. Examples show maps that return 0 or 1, and a note that x->a, y->a+b, z->c-a2+b3 gives is_surjective=1 in examples. See also help is injective/help is surjective for more interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: is_bijective
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: is bijective(phi,pr); phi map to basering, pr preimage ring. Return: an integer, 1 if phi is bijective, 0 if not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm checks first injectivity and then surjectivity. Interpretation for local/mixed orderings or for quotient rings should follow help is surjective and help is injective. A comment is displayed if printlevel >= voice-1 (default). Examples demonstrate cases: map not injective (returns 0), or map between quotient rings returning 1, or map injective but not surjective (returns 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: noetherNormal
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: noetherNormal(id[,p]); id ideal, p integer. Return: a list l of two ideals, say I,J: - I defines a map (coordinate change in the basering), such that: - J is generated by a subset of the variables with size(J) = dim(id). If we define map phi=basering,I; then k[var(1),...,var(n)]/phi(id) is finite over k[J]. If p is given, 0<=p<=100, a sparse coordinate change with p percent of the matrix entries being 0 (default: p=0 i.e. dense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed for characteristic 0. It can work in char k > 0 if it terminates, but may result in an infinite loop in small characteristic. Example shows output list of two ideals I and J and explicit linear combinations; the goal is to produce a coordinate change and a subset of variables that give a Noether normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: mapIsFinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: mapIsFinite(phi,R[,J]); R the preimage ring of the map phi: R -> basering. J an ideal in the basering, J = 0 if not given. Return: 1 if R -> basering/J is finite and 0 else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R may be a quotient ring (this will be ignored since a map R/I -> S/J is finite iff the induced map R -> S/J is finite). Example demonstrates a map and returns 1. See also finitenessTest for related tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: finitenessTest
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: finitenessTest(J[,v]); J ideal, v intvec (say v1,...,vr with vi>0). Return: a list l with l[1] integer, l[2], l[3], l[4] ideals: - l[1] = 1 if var(v1),...,var(vr) are in l[2] and 0 else. - l[2] (resp. l[3]) contains those variables which occur (resp. do not occur) as pure power in the leading term of one of the generators of J. - l[4] contains those J[i] for which the leading term is a pure power of a variable (which is then in l[2]). (default v = [1,2,..,nvars(basering)])
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory: If J is a standard basis of an ideal generated by x1 - f1(y),..., xn - fn with yj ordered lexicographically and yj >> xi, then if yi appears as pure power in the leading term of J[k], J[k] defines an integral relation for yi over the y(i+1),... and the f’s. Moreover, in this situation, if l[2] = y1,...,yr, then K[y1,...,yr] is finite over K[f1..fn]. If J contains furthermore polynomials hj(y), then K[y1,...,yz]/<hj> is finite over K[f1..fn]. References to Prop. 3.1.5 in the textbook are given. Examples show calls with std(i) and std(j) and list outputs separating variables and relations; many illustrative outputs shown in example block.

rubrics_metrics.name: nonZeroEntry
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: nonZeroEntry(id); id = object for which the test 'id[i]!=0', i=1,..,N, N=size(id) (resp. ncols(id) for id of type ideal or module) is defined (e.g. ideal, vector, list of polynomials, intvec,...). Return: a list, say l, with l[1] an integer, l[2], l[3] integer vectors: - l[1] number of non-zero entries of id. - l[2] intvec of size l[1] with l[2][i]=i if id[i] != 0 (in case l[1]!=0). - l[3] intvec with l[3][i]=1 if id[i]!=0 and l[3][i]=0 else. (l[2]=0 if l[1]=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show nonZeroEntry on leadexp(f) returning counts and index/intvec outputs, and using nonZeroEntry on a list L to return positions of non-zero entries. Useful for scanning objects to identify non-zero components; outputs include both index lists and indicator vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: zeroRadical
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage: zeroRadical(I[, exactness]); I ideal, exactness int. Assume: I is zero-dimensional in Q[variables]. Return: the radical of I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: A final test is applied to the result if exactness != 0 (default), otherwise no final test is done. Example given: zeroRadical(I) produces factors _[1]=y2-1, _[2]=x2-x for a sample ideal. Library: assprimeszerodim.lib — purpose is associated primes of a zero-dimensional ideal using modular computations. Authors and overview noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: assPrimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume: I is zero-dimensional over Q[variables]. Return: a list of the associated primes of I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: A final test is applied to the result if exactness != 0 (default), otherwise no final test is done. Example shows calling assPrimes(I) for a 6-variable ideal and extensive returned associated-prime list; outputs are ideals generating each associated prime. Cross-reference: See also primdec.lib (Section D.4.21).
